title: Abdominal pain and swelling in a 53-year-old dairy farmer
desc: This station involves a focused history and examination of a 53-year-old dairy farmer in a rural general practice. He has had 1 day of left lower quadrant pain that began suddenly as cramps and is now constant, with severe abdominal distension, early obstipation and late bilious vomiting. He has had diverticulitis before, had colonic polyps removed 5 years ago and never had the surveillance colonoscopy, and his father had colon cancer. The candidate then interprets two sets of observations (getting worse), a urine dipstick and his old colonoscopy report. They recognise probable large bowel obstruction, arrange urgent transfer to hospital, explain the causes of small and large bowel obstruction, and safety-net.
focus: Recognising large bowel obstruction from the history and examination, telling it apart from its differentials, and arranging safe, urgent transfer from general practice
diagnosis: Suspected colorectal cancer or diverticular stricture
stem: You are a medical student on placement at a rural general practice. Jeoff Cavalier, a 53-year-old dairy farmer, has come to the clinic with abdominal pain. Your supervising GP has asked you to see him first. A practice nurse is available.
tasks: Take a focused history from Mr Cavalier and perform a focused examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Mr Cavalier's observations, his urine dipstick result and the report of his colonoscopy from 5 years ago. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Jeoff Cavalier, a 53-year-old dairy farmer. You are a tough, plain-speaking bloke who rarely sees a doctor, so being here means you are really suffering. You sit very still with your hands on your swollen belly and wince when you move. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate uses medical words without explaining them, say: "Speak English, Doc."

Opening line: "Hey Doc, I've got some real bad pains in me stomach and it's completely blown up. It's the worst feeling in the world."

If asked to say more: "Been starting to feel pretty sick too."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Site: low down on the left side of your tummy (point to the left lower abdomen). It doesn't go anywhere else.
  • Onset: it came on suddenly yesterday morning, about a day ago, while you were milking.
  • Time course: at first it came and went in waves. Now it is there all the time. You have never had anything like it before.
  • Character: "It was crampy, now it's tight. Feels like I'm about to pop." It is not sharp, dull or burning.
  • Severity: 8 out of 10.
  • Nothing makes it better. You haven't taken anything for it.
  • Nothing set it off: no injury, no recent illness, nobody around you is sick, no change in what you eat. You admit you eat "not much fibre".

Tummy swelling and bowels (only if asked):

  • Your belly has blown up since yesterday and keeps getting bigger and tighter.
  • Your last bowel motion was yesterday morning: small and hard. You haven't passed any wind since last night.
  • Before this you were regular, once a day, with no recent change. No diarrhoea, no blood, no black poo, no mucus.

Vomiting (only if asked):

  • You vomited once, a large amount, in the past hour, just before you came in. It was food and then bitter green-yellow fluid (bile).
  • No blood, nothing like coffee grounds, no clots, and nothing that looked or smelt like poo.

Say no to all of these if asked:

  • Fevers, sweats, shakes or rigors.
  • Weight loss ("Jeans are still too tight"), loss of appetite before this, tiredness, breathlessness or looking pale.
  • Blood from the bottom, at any time.
  • Pain in the upper tummy or going through to the back, heartburn, yellow skin or eyes.
  • A lump in the groin or anywhere on the tummy.
  • A swollen belly like this before that settled on its own.
  • Crohn's disease or colitis, bloody diarrhoea, or antibiotics recently.
  • A racing or irregular heartbeat, or being told you have an irregular heart rhythm.
  • Pain or blood when passing urine, or pain in the loin.
  • Recent travel.

Past medical history:

  • Type 2 diabetes for 5 years.
  • High blood pressure for 6 years.
  • Diverticulitis: "a couple of bouts". The GP treated them with antibiotics and the last was about 2 years ago. The pain was in the same spot but "nothing like this", and your belly didn't swell up.
  • Bowel screening: 5 years ago the GP did a poo test, and it came back positive. You had a colonoscopy, which found "two or three polyps" that were removed. You can't remember what they said about another one, and you haven't had a colonoscopy or a poo test since.
  • Operations: you had your appendix out at 15 after a bad tummy pain. That is the only other bad pain you've had. No other operations.
  • No cancer and no hernias.

Medications: perindopril 5 mg daily; metformin (you're not sure of the dose); fish oil. Nothing else, and no anti-inflammatories or blood thinners. Your vaccinations are up to date.

Allergies: oxycodone ("came out in a bad rash all over"). Sticky tape also gives you a rash.

Family history: your mother died of old age. Your father died of colon cancer at 79. Your son and daughter are healthy.

Social history:

  • You smoked a pack a day for 20 years and quit 6 years ago.
  • Dairy farmer, very active. Fully independent.
  • Takeaway or fast food about 5 times a week.
  • You live with your wife, your adult son and his partner. Your son works the farm with you.
  • You catch up with mates at the pub. Only if asked how much: "a few beers on a Friday."
  • No drugs.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Ideas: "Thought it might be the diverticulitis again, but this is different."
  • Concern: "I'm worried it's something serious." Only if asked why: "Dad had bowel cancer."
  • Expectation: you want it sorted, and you want to get back for the afternoon milking.

Question to raise once in Part 1: "Is it something serious, Doc?"

If the candidate asks for tests in Part 1, say the nurse is checking his blood sugar and urine and the results will come shortly. If they offer pain relief, say the GP will give it once the assessment is finished.

Exam findings (examiner gives when the candidate says what they examine)

  • General: uncomfortable, lying still, grimacing when he shifts, visibly distended abdomen. Alert and talking. Weight 96 kg, height 178 cm (BMI 30).
  • Observations (09:40): temperature 37.4 °C, HR 108 regular, BP 134/82, RR 20, SpO2 97% on room air, CRT 3 seconds, pain 8/10. Capillary BGL: the nurse is doing it now; the result comes in Part 2.
  • Hydration: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, CRT 3 seconds.
  • Hands, eyes, neck: pulse regular. No clubbing or palmar pallor. Conjunctivae pink, no jaundice. No supraclavicular lymph nodes.
  • Chest and heart: chest clear. Heart sounds dual, no murmurs.
  • Abdomen, inspection: grossly and evenly distended, tense and shiny. Healed scar in the right iliac fossa (old appendicectomy). No visible peristalsis. No hernias visible on coughing. Coughing makes him wince because his belly is so tight, but there is no localised cough tenderness.
  • Abdomen, palpation: tender all over, worst in the left iliac fossa, with voluntary guarding there. Mild tenderness in the right iliac fossa. No rigidity and no rebound tenderness. No mass can be felt through the distension. Liver and spleen not palpable.
  • Abdomen, percussion: tympanic (hyper-resonant) throughout. No percussion tenderness. No shifting dullness.
  • Bowel sounds: present, high-pitched and tinkling.
  • Hernial orifices: inguinal and femoral orifices clear, including on cough. Scrotum normal.
  • Renal angles: non-tender.
  • Rectal examination (if offered, with a chaperone): empty rectum, no mass felt, no faeces, no blood or melaena on the glove.

check.x: Professionalism
Performs hand hygiene, introduces self, confirms Jeoff's identity and gains consent.
Acknowledges his severe pain early (offers a comfortable position and says analgesia will be arranged), uses plain language and responds honestly to his worry that it is serious.
History
Characterises the pain:

kids.x: Site and radiation: left lower quadrant, no radiation.
Onset and time course: sudden onset 1 day ago, episodic (colicky) at first and now constant, never had it before.
kids.d: The change from colicky to constant pain must be elicited.

kids.x: Character and severity: crampy, now tight ('about to pop'), 8/10.
Aggravating and relieving factors and triggers: nothing relieves it, no analgesia taken, no trauma, illness, contacts or change in diet.

check.x: Asks about the features of obstruction:

kids.x: Abdominal distension: severe and getting worse since yesterday.
Bowels and flatus: last motion yesterday morning (small and hard), no wind since last night, previously regular.
Vomiting: when it started in relation to the pain (late, in the past hour), how often (once, large), and what it contained (food then bile; no blood, coffee grounds or faeculent material).

check.x: Asks cluster questions to rule other causes in or out:
check.d: Award each kid on its own. Kid 3 is critical: award only if at least two of weight loss, rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit or anaemia symptoms are asked.

kids.x: Small bowel obstruction and hernia: early vomiting, central colicky pain, groin or abdominal lumps.
Diverticulitis or perforation: fever, sweats or rigors, previous episodes and how this compares.
Colorectal cancer: weight loss, rectal bleeding, change in bowel habit, symptoms of anaemia.

Ischaemic bowel, pancreatitis, toxic megacolon and volvulus: irregular heartbeat or vascular disease, pain out of proportion, bloody diarrhoea; epigastric pain to the back, alcohol, gallstones; IBD or recent antibiotics; previous episodes of distension that settled.
kids.d: Award for at least two of these four diagnoses.

check.x: Takes the past medical and surgical history:

kids.x: Type 2 diabetes for 5 years, hypertension for 6 years, previous bouts of diverticulitis.
Appendicectomy at 15, and no other operations or hernias (relevant to adhesions).
Bowel screening: positive FOBT 5 years ago, colonoscopy with 2 to 3 polyps removed, and no surveillance colonoscopy or FOBT since.

check.x: Takes a medication history: perindopril 5 mg daily, metformin, fish oil, no NSAIDs or anticoagulants, vaccinations up to date.
Asks about allergies and the reactions: oxycodone (widespread rash) and tape (rash).
Takes a family history: father died of colon cancer at 79, mother died of old age, son and daughter healthy.

Takes a social history: ex-smoker (a pack a day for 20 years, quit 6 years ago), dairy farmer, fast food 5 times a week and low-fibre diet, alcohol quantified, lives with wife, son and son's partner, independent.
check.d: Award for smoking, diet, alcohol and living situation.

check.x: Explores his ideas, concerns and expectations: thought it might be diverticulitis, worried it is serious because of his father, wants to get back for milking.
Examination
Asks for a full set of vital signs and a capillary BGL, notes the regular pulse, identifies the tachycardia (HR 108) and notes the temperature is upper-normal (37.4 °C).
check.d: Critical element: asks for a full set of vital signs and identifies the tachycardia (HR 108). Credit asking for the BGL and noting the 37.4 °C temperature, but these are not required for the critical mark.

check.x: Inspects generally and assesses hydration: lying still and distended, dry mucous membranes, reduced turgor, CRT 3 seconds; no pallor, jaundice or supraclavicular nodes.
Examines the abdomen:

kids.x: Inspection: gross symmetrical distension and the right iliac fossa appendicectomy scar.
Palpation, gently: tenderness worst in the left iliac fossa with guarding, mild right iliac fossa tenderness, and checks for peritonism (no rigidity or rebound).
kids.d: Credit percussion tenderness as the gentler test of peritonism.

kids.x: Percussion: tympanic throughout.
Auscultation: high-pitched, tinkling bowel sounds.

check.x: Examines the hernial orifices (clear) and offers a rectal examination with a chaperone (empty rectum, no mass, no blood).
check.d: Critical element: examines the hernial orifices. Credit offering a chaperoned rectal examination, or stating that it would be done before transfer or by the surgical team.

check.x: Summarises the findings: tachycardic, dry, grossly distended and tympanic abdomen with left-sided tenderness and guarding, obstructive bowel sounds, empty rectum, no peritonitis.
check.d: Award without 'empty rectum' if the rectal exam was deferred or declined; include it only if the rectal exam was performed and the finding was given.

check.x: Interpretation

Interprets the observations as getting worse over 35 minutes: HR up from 108 to 116, systolic BP down from 134 to 116, RR up from 20 to 22, temperature 37.6 °C, pain 9/10 and further vomiting. This means increasing hypovolaemia or early sepsis, so he needs hospital now by ambulance.
check.d: Critical element: identifies the rising HR (108 to 116) and falling systolic BP (134 to 116) as deterioration (hypovolaemia or early sepsis) needing hospital now by ambulance. Credit RR, temperature, pain and further vomiting, but these are not required for the critical mark.

check.x: Interprets BGL 12.6 mmol/L as stress hyperglycaemia and the urine (SG 1.030, ketones 2+) as dehydration and starvation ketosis.
check.d: Credit noting no blood, leucocytes or nitrites.

check.x: Interprets the colonoscopy report: previous adenomas (one advanced, 12 mm, sigmoid) and sigmoid diverticulosis, with 3-year surveillance missed, raising suspicion of a sigmoid cancer or diverticular stricture.

Gives large bowel obstruction as the most likely diagnosis and justifies it: left lower quadrant colicky then constant pain, gross distension, early obstipation, late vomiting, previous diverticulitis and colorectal cancer risk factors (adenomas, father's colon cancer, ex-smoker).

Gives at least three differentials with a feature for or against each (for example adhesional small bowel obstruction, complicated diverticulitis, sigmoid volvulus, toxic megacolon, mesenteric ischaemia).
Management

Recognises a surgical emergency, informs the supervising GP, phones the on-call surgical registrar or ED with a handover, and sends a referral letter with his medications, allergies (oxycodone, tape) and the colonoscopy report.
Arranges transfer by ambulance now because he is getting worse; he is not driven by his wife or allowed to drive himself.
Keeps him nil by mouth.

Offers analgesia that avoids oxycodone (e.g. fentanyl IV/intranasal or methoxyflurane as a bridge) and a non-prokinetic antiemetic (e.g. ondansetron), and does not give metoclopramide in mechanical obstruction.
check.d: Not awarded if the candidate proposes oxycodone, or metoclopramide. Accept fentanyl (IV or intranasal per practice protocol) as the preferred opioid because it is structurally unrelated to oxycodone; credit a candidate who says morphine and hydromorphone are avoided or used only with caution because of possible cross-reactivity. Accept methoxyflurane as a short bridge, noting caution if renal function may be impaired. Ondansetron 4 mg wafer or IM. Credit suggesting the GP insert a cannula (hypoallergenic dressing) and start an IV crystalloid bolus while awaiting the ambulance, per practice protocol.

check.x: Withholds metformin and perindopril while he is vomiting, dehydrated and likely to have IV contrast and surgery, and tells the hospital team.

Tells Jeoff what to expect in hospital: blood tests including lactate, a drip, a CT scan of the abdomen, possibly a tube through the nose to empty the stomach, and a surgical review that may lead to a stent or an operation.
check.d: Award for any three of: bloods, IV fluids, CT with contrast, nasogastric tube, surgical review with stent or operation.

check.x: Explains the causes of bowel obstruction:

kids.x: Small bowel: adhesions from previous surgery and incarcerated hernias are the main causes.
Large bowel: colorectal cancer, diverticular stricture and volvulus are the main causes.
For Jeoff: a sigmoid cancer, diverticular stricture or sigmoid volvulus fits (accept any, with reasoning); his appendicectomy adhesions would more often block the small bowel.

check.x: Answers 'Is it cancer like Dad?' honestly: cancer is possible and the scan and colonoscopy will tell, without falsely reassuring or confirming it.
Safety netting

Tells him and his wife to alert staff straight away if the pain suddenly gets much worse or spreads, his belly goes hard, he feels faint, cold or confused, he gets shakes, or he vomits brown foul-smelling fluid; staff will re-call 000 to upgrade the ambulance priority.
check.d: Award for at least three red flags in plain words, linked to alerting staff.

check.x: Keeps him in the treatment room with nurse observations every 15 minutes until the ambulance arrives.

part2.lead: While you were seeing Jeoff, the practice nurse checked his blood glucose and urine, and she has just repeated his observations. You have also found the report of his colonoscopy from 5 years ago in the practice records. Here they are.
part2.patient:
Put these once each, while the candidate explains the plan:

  • "What's blocking it, Doc? Is it cancer, like Dad had?"
  • "Do I really need an ambulance? The missus can drive me. And who's going to do the milking?"

You accept the ambulance if the candidate explains why (and that your son can do the milking). You are frightened but grateful for straight answers. If the candidate uses jargon such as "obstruction", "stricture" or "nasogastric" without explaining it, ask what it means.

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Room air throughout. First set at 09:40 on arrival; repeat set by the practice nurse at 10:15. Capillary BGL 12.6 mmol/L (nurse, 09:50). No medicines given yet.
handover.model:
• Read: general practice has no zoned observation chart, so read the trend. Over 35 minutes HR has risen from 108 to 116 and systolic BP has fallen from 134 to 116 (he takes perindopril). RR is up from 20 to 22, temperature 37.6 °C (low-grade, not a fever), pain up to 9/10, CRT 3 seconds, and he has vomited again. SpO2 normal, alert. Capillary BGL 12.6 mmol/L.
  • For Jeoff: increasing hypovolaemia from vomiting and fluid lost into the distended bowel, with or without an early inflammatory response. Constant pain with rising HR, and mild RIF tenderness (concern for caecal distension), raise concern for bowel ischaemia or impending perforation. The BGL is stress hyperglycaemia in type 2 diabetes.
  • What it changes: he needs hospital now, by ambulance, nil by mouth, with repeat observations while he waits. A further fall in BP, confusion, rigors or a rigid abdomen means suspected perforation or sepsis, and staff re-call 000 to upgrade the ambulance priority. Hold metformin and perindopril, and the hospital monitors his BGL.

rows.note: Repeat set; vomited bile once in the treatment room

handover.label: Urine dipstick
handover.result: Urine sample, dipstick tested at the practice at 09:55.
handover.model:
• Read: specific gravity 1.030 (top of the strip), ketones 2+, glucose 1+. No blood, leucocytes, nitrites, protein or bilirubin.
  • For Jeoff: concentrated urine and ketones show dehydration and starvation from vomiting and not eating. The glucose fits his raised BGL. No blood argues against a ureteric stone; no leucocytes or nitrites argue against urinary infection (and against a colovesical fistula from diverticular disease).
  • What it changes: it supports IV fluids in hospital and withholding metformin and perindopril. Ketonuria with hyperglycaemia: check capillary or blood ketones if a meter is available, and the hospital venous gas will exclude ketoacidosis (unlikely, as he is not on an SGLT2 inhibitor). It does not help confirm or exclude obstruction.

handover.label: Colonoscopy and histology report (5 years ago)
handover.result:
Procedure: colonoscopy under sedation, 5 years ago.

Indication: positive iFOBT requested by GP (father with colon cancer). 48-year-old man.

Preparation: good. Caecum reached and confirmed (appendicectomy, appendiceal orifice puckered); terminal ileum intubated.

Findings:

  • Terminal ileum and caecum: normal.
  • Transverse colon: one 5 mm sessile polyp, removed by cold snare.
  • Descending colon: one 4 mm sessile polyp, removed by cold snare.
  • Sigmoid colon: moderate diverticulosis with some muscular thickening; no stricture, the scope passed easily. One 12 mm pedunculated polyp at 30 cm, removed by hot snare; base clear.
  • Rectum: normal.

Histology: all three polyps are tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia. The 12 mm adenoma is completely excised. No high-grade dysplasia or malignancy.

Conclusion: three tubular adenomas with low-grade dysplasia, one advanced by size (12 mm, sigmoid), all excised; moderate sigmoid diverticulosis. Surveillance at 3 years.

Practice note: recall letter sent 2 years ago; no colonoscopy recorded since.
handover.model:
• Read: three tubular adenomas, one advanced (≥10 mm), which is why 3-year surveillance was advised; all removed, with no high-grade dysplasia or cancer. Moderate sigmoid diverticulosis with muscular thickening. He is now 2 years overdue for surveillance.
  • For Jeoff: a history of adenomas, especially a large one, puts him at higher risk of a new colorectal cancer, and a cancer can develop in the 5 years since. Sigmoid diverticular disease with previous diverticulitis can cause a fibrotic stricture. Both point to the sigmoid colon, which fits left lower quadrant pain and an empty rectum.
  • What it changes: it raises suspicion of a sigmoid cancer or diverticular stricture as the cause of a large bowel obstruction. Send the report with him. He will need CT and, when safe, colonoscopy with biopsy, and the missed surveillance should be raised gently and documented.

ask: You are now calling the on-call general surgical registrar at the regional hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Jeoff Cavalier, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Jeoff now, here in general practice.

Jeoff asks what could be blocking his bowel. Briefly tell me the main causes of small and large bowel obstruction and which fits Jeoff, then what you would tell him and his wife while he waits for the ambulance.
expect:
• Identify: self (medical student with the GP), the practice; Jeoff Cavalier, 53, dairy farmer.
  • Situation: suspected large bowel obstruction, getting worse; requesting urgent surgical review; ambulance arranged.
  • Background: 1 day sudden LLQ pain, colicky then constant; gross distension; no flatus since last night; late bilious vomiting x2. Previous diverticulitis; colonoscopy 5 years ago: 3 adenomas, one 12 mm in the sigmoid, plus sigmoid diverticulosis; 3-year surveillance missed; father colon cancer; appendicectomy. T2DM (metformin), HTN (perindopril). Allergies: oxycodone (rash), tape (rash).
  • Assessment: tense, tympanic abdomen, left iliac fossa tenderness and guarding, mild RIF tenderness (concern for caecal distension), no peritonitis, tinkling bowel sounds, empty rectum. HR up from 108 to 116, SBP down from 134 to 116, RR 20 to 22, T 37.6, pain 9/10, vomited again, BGL 12.6; urine ketones 2+, SG 1.030: dehydrated and deteriorating.
  • Recommendation: accept for urgent review; NBM; bloods with lactate and VBG (exclude ketoacidosis), IV fluids, CT with contrast; metformin and perindopril held.

Most likely: large bowel obstruction, probably from a sigmoid cancer or a diverticular stricture. Supporting features: left lower quadrant colicky then constant pain, gross distension, early obstipation, late vomiting, tympanic abdomen with tinkling bowel sounds, empty rectum; adenomas with missed surveillance, father's colon cancer, ex-smoker, previous diverticulitis.

  • Adhesional small bowel obstruction: for: previous appendicectomy, vomiting. Against: vomiting late, early obstipation, left-sided pain.
  • Complicated diverticulitis: for: previous episodes, left iliac fossa tenderness and guarding. Against: no fever; distension and obstipation dominate.
  • Sigmoid volvulus: for: sudden onset, gross distension. Against: no previous episodes; needs imaging.
  • Toxic megacolon: against: no bloody diarrhoea, IBD or antibiotics.

1. Surgical emergency: tell the supervising GP; phone the surgical registrar or ED; letter with medications, allergies and the colonoscopy report.
  2. Ambulance now (HR rising, BP falling), not a private car.
  3. Nil by mouth.
  4. Analgesia: fentanyl or methoxyflurane; avoid oxycodone and related opioids. Ondansetron, not metoclopramide.
  5. IV access with a hypoallergenic dressing and an IV crystalloid bolus started by the GP while awaiting the ambulance, per practice protocol.
  6. Withhold metformin and perindopril.
  7. Explain hospital plan: bloods, drip, CT, possibly a nose tube, surgeon review.

• Causes: SBO: adhesions, hernia. LBO: cancer, diverticular stricture, volvulus. Jeoff: sigmoid cause (cancer, diverticular stricture or volvulus).
  • Cancer question: answer honestly: cancer is possible; the CT and colonoscopy will tell.
  • While he waits: stays in the treatment room with nurse observations every 15 minutes until the ambulance arrives.
  • Red flags (he and his wife alert staff straight away; staff re-call 000 to upgrade the ambulance priority): pain much worse or spreading, or belly hard; faint, cold or confused; vomiting brown foul-smelling fluid.
  • Extra credit: shakes or rigors; clammy skin.

ddx.dx: Large bowel obstruction, most likely from a sigmoid colon cancer or a diverticular stricture
ddx.for: Sudden left lower quadrant colicky pain now constant, gross tympanic distension, early obstipation, late vomiting, empty rectum, previous diverticulitis, adenomas with missed surveillance and a father with colon cancer.
ddx.against: No weight loss, rectal bleeding or change in bowel habit before this episode.

ddx.for: Sudden onset with rapid, gross distension and left-sided colicky pain with early obstipation.
ddx.against: No previous episodes of distension that settled, and he is younger and more active than the typical patient; it cannot be excluded without imaging.

ddx.for: Previous appendicectomy, colicky pain, distension and bilious vomiting.
ddx.against: Vomiting came late (only after a day), obstipation came early, and the pain is in the left lower quadrant rather than central.

ddx.for: Previous diverticulitis, sigmoid diverticulosis on colonoscopy, left iliac fossa tenderness with guarding and a low-grade temperature (37.6 °C).
ddx.against: No true fever (≥38 °C) or rigors, and gross distension with absolute obstipation is far more than his previous bouts.
No bloody diarrhoea, no IBD, no recent antibiotics, and he is obstipated rather than having diarrhoea.

ddx.for: Severe constant pain, rising heart rate, and vascular risk factors (diabetes, hypertension, ex-smoker).
ddx.against: Regular pulse with no history of AF, no bloody diarrhoea, and abdominal signs that match the pain.

guide:
This is a general practice station, so there is no observation chart. Give the first set of observations from the Exam findings when the candidate asks for them. The capillary BGL is being done by the nurse and is given in Part 2. In Part 1 the examiner gives findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate asks for blood tests or imaging, say these would be done in hospital. The nurse repeats the observations at 10:15 whatever the candidate does, and no medicines are given before then. In Part 2 hand over all three results, then ask the four questions in order. Jeoff asks his two questions once each while the candidate explains the plan.

Credit cluster questions per item 7; colorectal cancer red flags must be asked specifically.

A high-performing candidate characterises the pain and picks up the change from colicky to constant pain. They separate large from small bowel obstruction by the order of symptoms (early obstipation, late vomiting, distension), screen widely for differentials and cancer red flags, and find the polyps with missed surveillance, the father's colon cancer and the oxycodone allergy. They examine gently for peritonism, the hernial orifices and the rectum. In Part 2 they see that he is getting worse and send him by ambulance, nil by mouth, with safe analgesia and antiemetic choices and his diabetes and blood pressure medicines held. They explain the causes clearly and answer the cancer question honestly.

A borderline candidate calls it diverticulitis or constipation and plans oral antibiotics, laxatives or review tomorrow. They may give oxycodone or metoclopramide, let his wife drive him, miss the deterioration, or fail to ask about bowels and flatus.
explain:
Diagnosis

Jeoff most likely has a large bowel obstruction (LBO), probably at the sigmoid colon. His left lower quadrant pain began suddenly and was colicky (peristalsis against a blockage) and is now constant and tight, which signals increasing distension and possibly ischaemia. He has gross tympanic distension, has passed no flatus or stool since early in the illness, and vomited only late. The rectum is empty, and bowel sounds are tinkling. His background points to the cause: three adenomas 5 years ago with missed surveillance, a father with colon cancer, an ex-smoker with a low-fibre diet and obesity, and recurrent sigmoid diverticulitis. The sudden onset while milking, with gross distension within a day and no change in bowel habit beforehand, fits a sigmoid volvulus just as well; an obstructing cancer or a diverticular stricture usually comes on more gradually. Imaging in hospital tells these apart, and any of the three is a reasonable answer when the reasoning is given.

Small versus large bowel obstruction

Small bowelLarge bowel
PainCentral, colicky, frequent wavesLower abdominal, less frequent colic
VomitingEarly and prominent, biliousLate, may become faeculent
DistensionMild to moderate (more if distal)Marked
ObstipationLateEarly

A competent ileocaecal valve turns an LBO into a closed loop: the colon cannot decompress backwards, and the caecum, the widest and thinnest-walled part, distends most and can become ischaemic and perforate. Right iliac fossa tenderness in a patient with LBO is therefore a warning sign, as are constant pain, fever, tachycardia, peritonism and a rising lactate.

Causes

  • Small bowel obstruction: adhesions from previous surgery (most common) and incarcerated hernias; also tumours, Crohn's strictures, gallstone ileus and intussusception.
  • Large bowel obstruction: colorectal cancer (most common), diverticular stricture and volvulus (sigmoid, less often caecal); also adhesions, IBD strictures, faecal impaction and foreign bodies. Acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie syndrome) mimics LBO without a mechanical cause, usually in unwell inpatients.

Differentials that matter

  • Adhesional SBO: his appendicectomy makes adhesions possible, but the order of symptoms fits the large bowel.
  • Complicated diverticulitis: previous episodes and left iliac fossa tenderness, but no true fever, and the obstruction dominates. Repeated diverticulitis can cause a fibrotic stricture, and on CT it can be hard to tell from cancer. Therapeutic Guidelines manages complicated diverticulitis (abscess, perforation, obstruction) in hospital with intravenous antibiotics, not with oral antibiotics in the community.
  • Sigmoid volvulus: sudden onset and gross distension; a 'coffee bean' on X-ray or a whirl sign on CT.
  • Toxic megacolon and mesenteric ischaemia: must not be missed, but he has no bloody diarrhoea, IBD, antibiotics or AF.

Interpreting the results

  • Observations: HR up and systolic BP down within 35 minutes, with pain rising and further vomiting. He is losing fluid into the bowel and by vomiting, and may be developing ischaemia. He must go by ambulance.
  • BGL and urine: stress hyperglycaemia, ketones and concentrated urine show dehydration and starvation ketosis; no blood or leucocytes. Ketonuria with hyperglycaemia in a person with diabetes should prompt a capillary or blood ketone check if a meter is available, and the hospital venous gas will exclude ketoacidosis (unlikely, as he is not on an SGLT2 inhibitor).
  • Colonoscopy: adenomas (one advanced by size, 12 mm) and sigmoid diverticulosis, with 3-year surveillance recommended but not done. A cancer may have developed in the interval, and the diverticular disease can stricture. The ACSQHC Colonoscopy Clinical Care Standard expects surveillance to follow NHMRC-approved guidelines, with recall systems in place.

Imaging in hospital

CT of the abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the investigation of choice. It confirms obstruction, finds the transition point and cause, and shows complications (ischaemia, perforation, caecal diameter). If cancer is suspected it also helps staging. A plain abdominal X-ray may show dilated colon with haustra (the '3-6-9' rule: small bowel over 3 cm, colon over 6 cm, caecum over 9 cm is abnormal) but rarely shows the cause.

Management

In general practice: this is a surgical emergency. Phone the surgical registrar or ED, send a letter with his medicines, allergies and the colonoscopy report, keep him nil by mouth, and transfer him by ambulance. Offer analgesia that avoids oxycodone (he had a widespread rash). Fentanyl (IV or intranasal) is the preferred opioid because it is structurally unrelated to oxycodone, whereas morphine and hydromorphone are phenanthrenes like oxycodone and are avoided or used only with caution (Australian Medicines Handbook, opioid hypersensitivity and cross-reactivity), and methoxyflurane can bridge briefly but needs caution if renal function may be impaired, as it may be in this dehydrated man on an ACE inhibitor. Choose an antiemetic such as ondansetron: metoclopramide is a prokinetic and is contraindicated in mechanical bowel obstruction (Australian Medicines Handbook). He is allergic to tape, so a hypoallergenic dressing is needed for any cannula, and the GP may start an IV crystalloid bolus while awaiting the ambulance. Under sick-day principles (ADEA), stop metformin while he is vomiting and dehydrated (it also matters for IV contrast and surgery), and withhold perindopril, which can worsen hypotension and acute kidney injury.

In hospital: FBC, UEC, LFTs, lipase, CRP, venous gas with lactate, group and hold; IV fluid resuscitation and electrolyte correction; nasogastric decompression if he is vomiting; a catheter for fluid balance; BGL monitoring; early surgical review. For obstructing left colon cancer, WSES guidance describes emergency resection (Hartmann's procedure, or resection with anastomosis with or without a diverting stoma) or a colonic stent as a bridge to elective surgery in selected patients. Signs of perforation or ischaemia need an emergency laparotomy. Sigmoid volvulus without ischaemia is usually decompressed endoscopically first. A colonoscopy with biopsy (when safe) and staging follow if a tumour is found.

Family history and screening

One first-degree relative diagnosed with colorectal cancer at 55 or older puts a person in the near-average risk category in the Cancer Council Australia/NHMRC guidelines. If Jeoff is diagnosed with colorectal cancer before 55, his son and daughter move into a higher category and need earlier, more intensive screening.

Safety netting

While he waits for the ambulance, he stays in the treatment room with nurse observations every 15 minutes. He and his wife should alert staff straight away if the pain suddenly worsens or spreads, his abdomen goes hard, he becomes faint, cold, clammy or confused, he has rigors, or he vomits brown, foul-smelling fluid; these suggest perforation or sepsis, and staff will re-call 000 to upgrade the ambulance priority. If he is sent home from hospital without surgery, he should return if the pain, distension or vomiting comes back or he stops passing wind. After discharge, the GP reviews his results, restarts metformin and perindopril once he is eating and his kidney function is known, and makes sure the colonoscopy and any cancer follow-up happen.
points: Large bowel obstruction gives early obstipation, marked distension and late vomiting; small bowel obstruction gives early vomiting, central colic and late obstipation.

Colicky pain that becomes constant, caecal (right iliac fossa) tenderness, fever, rising heart rate or falling blood pressure suggest ischaemia or impending perforation, especially with a competent ileocaecal valve.
The main causes of large bowel obstruction are colorectal cancer, diverticular stricture and volvulus; the main causes of small bowel obstruction are adhesions and hernias.
Previous adenomas with missed surveillance colonoscopy, a family history of colon cancer, smoking and a low-fibre diet raise the suspicion of an obstructing cancer.

In general practice: refer urgently with a handover, keep the patient nil by mouth, transfer by ambulance, give analgesia that respects allergies, give ondansetron rather than metoclopramide, and withhold metformin and ACE inhibitors.
CT abdomen and pelvis with IV contrast is the key hospital investigation; management ranges from decompression and stenting to emergency resection.
